en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk 11.
The Training Rule on Silk.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks approached the silk-weavers and said to them:
"Friends, weave much silk; give some to us as well, for we too wish to have a blanket made mixed with silk."
They complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, come to us and say:
‘Friends, weave many silk cloths; give some to us as well, for we too wish to have a rug made mixed with silk’?”
"It is our misfortune, it is our ill-gain, that for the sake of our livelihood and for the sake of our wives and children, we cause many small living beings to meet their destruction.
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... they complained, grumbled, and lamented:
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks approach silk-weavers and say, ‘Friends, weave much silk;
give some to us as well, for we too wish to have a rug made mixed with silk’?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that you approached the silk-weavers and said to them:
‘Friends, weave much silk; give some to us as well, for we also wish to have a rug made mixed with silk’?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, having approached the weavers of kosiya cloth, speak to them thus?”
“‘Friends, weave many silk-cloth garments; give some to us as well, for we too wish to have a rug made mixed with silk.
‘This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:”
“Whichever bhikkhu should have a rug made mixed with silk, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Whoever, however, means whoever of such a kind... [etc.]
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the meaning of "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Santhataṃ" (a rug) means:
"It has been made by weaving" means it is not woven.

"Should have it made" means that if one mixes even a single thread of *kosiya* silk and either makes it oneself or has it made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of undertaking.
By the mere acquisition [of it], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
"... [as before] ... Venerable sir, this blanket of mine, made by mixing in silk, is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha... [as before] ...
"Should give" means ...
"they should give" means ...
"I give to the Venerable One."
If one finishes by oneself what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one has others finish what was begun by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one finishes by oneself what was begun by others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one has another finish what was begun by others, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If one makes it for another’s purpose or has it made, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one uses something that was made by another and obtained [by oneself], it is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one makes a canopy, or a floor-covering, or a screen-wall, or a mattress, or a pillow;
or if one is insane.
"For the first offender":
the first training rule on silk is concluded.
